_readme: EXTERNAL MCP SERVERS the served model can call. Read by harness/mcp_server/bridge.py.
WHAT DOES NOT BELONG HERE: this repo's OWN server (`python -m harness.mcp_server`).
It was the only entry until 2026-07-31 and it was a LOOP — it exposes the same
harness skills she already has natively, so 9 of its 10 tools were shadowed and
skipped, and the net gain was `disk_free`, an EXAMPLE function in a file whose
docstring literally says 'Example:'. Two and a quarter seconds per call to reach a
five-line helper she could already have written in run_python.
harness/mcp_server IS STILL WORTH HAVING — it just points the other way. It is the
OUTBOUND surface: how Claude Code, LM Studio, or any MCP client reaches HER memory
and skills. See docs/MCP.md. The gate fixture that still needs a self-connection
lives at fixtures/mcp/selftest.json.
Per-server keys: `allow` (whitelist), `deny` (blacklist), `env`, `cwd`,
`inherit_env`, `remote_ok`. A bridged tool whose name a native tool owns is
NAMESPACED to <server>_<name>, never dropped — and as of 2026-08-25 that is
finally TRUE, because it was not before: the
bridge was spliced mid-assembly, so the nine packs below it lost any name an
external server had taken. G-MCP-SHADOW holds it now.
WHAT A SPAWNED SERVER SEES (2026-08-25). A child gets what an interpreter needs to
START on this platform, plus exactly what its `env` block declares. Nothing else —
not SP_XAI_API_KEY, not SP_RECALL_REGISTRY, which is the path to every fact she has
ever stored. Until today each child got `dict(os.environ)`, which is to say a package
resolved from the network at spawn time ran with her keys in its environment. A
server that genuinely needs the harness environment declares `"inherit_env": true`
and says why; the only one that does is our OWN server in the gate fixture.
AND PINNING. Every bridged tool's name + description + schema is fingerprinted on
first sight, and a tool whose fingerprint later CHANGES is refused by name. The
description is prompt — it is the sentence the model reads when deciding what a tool
does — so a same-name description swap is a complete exfiltration primitive that
changes nothing a human would notice. Trust on first use: it cannot vouch for the
FIRST listing, only that yesterday's offer is today's. Accept a change with
`python tools/mcp_pin.py --accept <server> <tool>`; SP_MCP_PIN=0 disarms it.
A REMOTE SERVER IS A DECISION, NOT A URL (2026-08-25). A {"url": ...} server on
loopback is another process on his machine and is fine. Anything else is REFUSED
unless that block says "remote_ok": true, and plain http to a non-loopback host
is refused even then — her tool arguments would cross the network in clear and
she has memory tools. This is NOT authorization: OAuth 2.1 + PKCE + resource
indicators is unbuilt, so a remote server he DOES allow is unauthenticated.
Ledgered in docs/OFF-BY-DEFAULT.md §7b rather than implied by a guard that
looks like more than it is.
ON `@latest`, SAID PLAINLY: the browser server is resolved from npm at spawn time and
is NOT version-pinned. Pinning the fingerprints bounds what a new build may change
about the SURFACE she is offered; it says nothing about the code behind it. Left
unpinned deliberately — chrome-devtools-mcp tracks Chrome, and a stale pin here is a
browser that silently stops working — and recorded here rather than left implied.

_why: A REAL browser, which is the one thing her web tools could not do. web_search
and web_fetch READ a page; this one can open it, click, fill a form, and see
what came back. --headless --isolated means it needs no pre-running Chrome and
leaves no profile behind.
TELEMETRY OFF, DELIBERATELY. chrome-devtools-mcp sends usage statistics to
Google, and trace URLs to the CrUX API, BY DEFAULT. This is his machine and her
browsing; neither flag is a preference.
`allow` keeps 7 of its 29 tools. The rest are lighthouse audits, performance
traces and heap snapshots — real tools, just not ones she has any use for, and
every entry in the load-on-demand index costs prompt budget whether she ever
calls it or not.
take_screenshot collides with her native sight tool, so it arrives as
browser_take_screenshot. Native keeps the bare name.
THE VERSION IS PINNED, AND `@latest` IS WHY (2026-08-28). npm resolved a new
chrome-devtools-mcp whenever the cache felt like it — six versions landed on this
machine between February and August — and each resolution changed the tools'
advertised schemas, so the fingerprint guard fired and REFUSED them. On 2026-08-26
that took out five of the seven tools in `allow`: navigate_page, take_snapshot,
take_screenshot, click and fill. She could open a page and list pages and nothing
else, and the log said `rug-pull` once per tool per listing while the real cause
was a floating specifier in this file.
The pins were made at 1.6.0 — 28 of 29 pinned digests reproduce there exactly,
against 4 at 1.8.0 — so pinning the version restores all five without accepting
anything on trust.
WHAT 1.8.0 ACTUALLY CHANGED, since the guard itself could not say: it adds a
`pageId` parameter ("Targets a specific page by ID.") to the page-scoped tools and
makes it REQUIRED. A real upstream feature, not a rug-pull — no description gained
instructions — but REQUIRED means her calls fail without it, so moving up is a
piece of work rather than an acceptance. Upgrade deliberately: change the version
here, run `python tools/mcp_pin.py --diff browser` to read what moved, then accept.
